items.answer: Sardar Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha, Bhagat Singh belonged to the Hindustan Socialist Republican Army and C.R. items.stem: Which of the following was the reason for calling off 'the Non-cooperation Movement' by Gandhiji?

options.label: B
options.text: Second Round Table Conference

options.label: C

items.answer: In February 1922 a crowd at Chauri-Chaura set fire to a police station and killed the policemen inside. Because the movement had turned violent and Gandhiji insisted that satyagraha must remain non-violent, he withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement. Hence the reason is the Chauri-Chaura incident.

items.assertion: Rich peasants became enthusiastic supporters of the Civil Disobedience Movement, organising their communities and at times forcing reluctant members to participate in the boycott programmes.
items.reason: However, they were deeply happy when the movement was called off in 1931 with revenue rates being lowered.
items.answer: Rich peasants such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh did throw themselves into the Civil Disobedience Movement and pressed their communities to join the boycott, so the assertion is true. But when the movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised, they were deeply disappointed, not happy. The reason is therefore false, so the assertion is true but the reason is false.

items.answer: The movement in the cities did slow down, because khadi was costly, Indian institutions were slow to come up and students and teachers drifted back to government schools, so the assertion is true. items.stem: Describe the role of Alluri Sitaram Raju in Andhra Pradesh during 1920s.
items.answer: Alluri Sitaram Raju led the Gudem rebels of the Andhra hills in the 1920s. He claimed a variety of special powers — that he could make correct astrological predictions, heal people and even survive bullet shots — and the rebels, captivated by him, proclaimed that he was an incarnation of God. He spoke of the greatness of Mahatma Gandhi, was inspired by the Non-Cooperation Movement and persuaded people to give up drinking and wear khadi. However, he also asserted that India could be liberated only by the use of force and not by non-violence, and under him the Gudem rebels attacked police stations, attempted to kill British officials and carried on guerrilla warfare to achieve Swaraj.

items.stem: Why did the British Government appoint the Simon Commission ?
items.answer: The Simon Commission was appointed by the British Government to fulfil its constitutional aspirations. Firstly, the Commission was to look into the working of the Government of India Act of 1919 and report on its success and failure in India. Secondly, it was to submit a list of suggestions that were essential for making political changes in India. However, this commission was appointed without any representation from India.

items.stem: Describe in brief the reactions of the people immediately after Jallianwalla Bagh incident.
items.answer: As the news of Jallianwalla Bagh spread, crowds took to the streets in many north Indian towns. There were strikes, clashes with the police and attacks on government buildings. The government responded with brutal repression, seeking to humiliate and terrorise the people, while the satyagrahis resisted with courage.

items.stem: Why did large sections of Muslims could not respond to the call for a united struggle through Civil Disobedience Movement ?
items.answer: Large sections of Muslims could not respond to the call for a united struggle through the Civil Disobedience Movement because they felt themselves alienated from the Congress after the decline of the Non-Cooperation Khilafat Movement, and because they feared that their culture and identity would be submerged under the domination of a Hindu majority.

items.stem: How did the revival of Indian folklore help to develop the ideas of nationalism ?
items.answer: National folk gave a true picture of traditional culture that had been corrupted by outside forces, national folk songs were helpful in discovering one's national identity, and together they helped in restoring a sense of pride in one's own past. In this way the revival of Indian folklore nourished the ideas of nationalism.

items.stem: What do you know about the Civil Disobedience Movement ?
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement was a movement revealing negligence of and defiance towards the British laws, and it was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in April 1930. It was the first successful mass movement, in which people from all sections took part — students, and people both young and old, joined it.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement ?
items.answer: Some activists of the Non-Cooperation Movement set a police station on fire at Chauri-Chaura (Gorakhpur) in Uttar Pradesh, in which 21 policemen were burnt alive. Because of this foolishness a peaceful non-violent movement turned into an ugly violent one. Mahatma Gandhi, the priest of non-violence, therefore decided immediately to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Why did the Muslims fail to respond to, the call of unified struggle during Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain.
items.answer: During the Civil Disobedience Movement the Muslims did not take part in the unified struggle. The main reason was that in 1933 Rehmat Ali uttered the word Pakistan at a meeting, which fed narrow and selfish feelings in the hearts of Muslims. It was accepted by Mohammad Ali Jinnah, the leader of the Mohammadans of Bharat, who placed these feelings before the Muslims of India. On this basis most Muslims decided not to take part in the Civil Disobedience Movement.

items.stem: “The Congress was reluctant to include the demands of industrial workers in its programme of struggle.” Analyse the reasons.
items.answer: The industrial working classes did not participate in the Civil Disobedience Movement in large numbers except in the Nagpur region. In 1930 thousands of workers in the Chhotanagpur tin mines wore Gandhi caps and took part in protest rallies and boycott campaigns. But the Congress was reluctant to include the workers' demands as part of its programme of struggle because it felt that this would alienate the industrialists, and it also hoped to avoid dividing the anti-imperial forces.

items.stem: Mention any three efforts made by Gandhiji to get Harijans their rights.
items.answer: Gandhiji called the untouchables Harijans, that is, the children of God. He organised satyagraha to secure them entry into temples and access to public wells, tanks and schools. He also persuaded the upper castes to change their heart and give up the sin of untouchability.

items.answer: Gandhiji perceived salt as a powerful symbol that could unite the nation because salt was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike, because it was the most essential item of food, and because the tax on salt and the government monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule.

items.stem: What led to the spread of Non-Cooperation movement to the countryside ? Explain any three factors.
items.answer: In the countryside the peasants had to do begar at the landlord's farm without any payment; the peasants demanded a reduction of land revenue and the abolition of begar; and the tenants had no security of tenure and were regularly evicted from the land. These grievances drew the peasants into the Non-Cooperation Movement and spread it to the countryside.

items.stem: When and where was Khilafat Committee formed ? What was its objective ?
items.answer: The Khilafat Committee was formed in March 1919 in Bombay. Its objectives were to defend the temporal powers of the Khalifa of Turkey, the spiritual head of the Islamic world, and to avert the harsh peace treaty that was about to be imposed on the Ottoman empire.

items.stem: Who designed the Swaraj Flag ? What were the features of this flag ? How was it used as a symbol of defiance ?
items.answer: In 1921 Gandhiji designed the Swaraj Flag. It was a tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre, representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help. Carrying the flag and holding it aloft during marches became a symbol of defiance.

items.stem: Explain the ideas of Gandhiji as he expressed in the famous book ‘Hind Swaraj’ regarding Non-Cooperation.
items.answer: In Hind Swaraj Gandhiji explained why British rule had succeeded in India and how the Non-Cooperation Movement could make it collapse. In his view British rule had been established in India with the co-operation of Indians and had survived only because of that co-operation; if Indians refused to cooperate, British rule would collapse within a year; and the success of the Non-Cooperation Movement would therefore bring Swaraj to the Indian people.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi choose ‘Salt Tax’ to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement ? Explain three reasons.
items.answer: Salt was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food; the tax on salt and the government monopoly over its production, as Mahatma Gandhi declared, revealed the most oppressive face of British rule; and all classes within Indian society could identify with it, so that everyone could be brought together in a united campaign. For these reasons Gandhiji chose the salt tax to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement.

items.answer: Natesa Sastri published a massive four volume collection of Tamil folk tales called The Folklore of Southern India. In many places local leaders told the peasants that Gandhiji had declared that no taxes were to be paid and that land was to be redistributed among the poor. The name of the Mahatma was thus being invoked to sanction all their actions and aspirations.

items.stem: Describe the incidence of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
items.answer: The famous Jallianwala Bagh incident took place on 13 April. A large crowd had gathered in the enclosed grounds of Jallianwala Bagh to make a peaceful protest against the repressive measures of the government and also to attend the annual Baisakhi fair. Being from outside the city, many villagers were unaware of the martial law that had been imposed. General Dyer entered the area, blocked all the exit points and opened fire on the innocent crowd, killing hundreds.

items.stem: Explain the reasons for relaunching the Civil Disobedience Movement by Gandhiji.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement was relaunched in 1932. The reasons were the failure of the talks at the Second Round Table Conference; the unrest through which the country was passing, with strikes by railway workers in 1930 and dock workers in 1932 and peasants facing high taxation and poverty; and the refusal of the Viceroy to meet Gandhiji or to take any step to relieve the measures affecting the people. For these reasons Gandhiji relaunched the Civil Disobedience Movement.

items.stem: Describe any two suggestive measures taken by the British administration to clamp down on nationalists.
items.answer: Two measures suggested by the British administration were the Government of India Act of 1935 and the Cripps Mission. Under the Act of 1935 the provinces and princely states were given autonomy to decide their own government and draft a constitution for governance; the Congress Committee rejected this act because under it the elected members were ineffective and unreal. The Cripps Mission was sent to India in March 1942 under the chairmanship of Sir Stafford Cripps to win the co-operation of the Indian people in the Second World War, at a time when the British position had become very precarious due to Hitler's attack.

items.stem: Discuss the role of women in the revolutionary movement.
items.answer: Women led by Surya Sen raided the port of Chittagong on 18 April 1930 and seized the armoury; among them were Pritilata Wadedar, Kalpana Dutt, Suniti Chaudhary and Shanti Ghose. Pritilata attacked the European club in Chittagong, was injured and committed suicide to escape arrest. Suniti Chaudhary and Shanti Ghose shot dead the District Magistrate of Tripura, and in Calcutta University Bina Das made an attempt on the life of Stanley Jackson, the Governor of Bengal.

items.stem: What was the impact of the First World War on the economic conditions in India ?
items.answer: The British were on one of the two sides in the war, and the war created huge expenditure on arms that forced the government to generate more revenue by imposing taxes. Custom duty and other taxes were increased, and it was for the first time that the British government introduced income tax. In these ways the First World War worsened the economic condition of India.

items.stem: Discuss the role of South India in the Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: In South India the Non-Cooperation Movement saw the opening of national schools in the Madras Presidency and the boycott of work at the Carnatic Textile Mills. The movement was conducted by C. Rajagopalachari in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and was also led by T. Prakasam and P. Sitaramayya.

items.stem: Why did Gandhiji decide to withdraw the ‘Non-Cooperation Movement’ in February, 1922? Explain any three reasons.
items.answer: Some activists of the Non-Cooperation Movement set a police station on fire at Chauri-Chaura (Gorakhpur) in Uttar Pradesh, in which 21 policemen were burnt alive. Gandhiji felt that the people of India were not yet ready for a nation-wide movement of mass struggle and that he should therefore withdraw the movement. Moreover, many members of the Indian National Congress felt that the Non-Cooperation Movement was tiresome and unnecessary, since they wanted to contest the elections.

items.answer: According to Gandhiji the social elements that are against democratic values are communalism, casteism in politics, religious communalism, election on the basis of communalism, and favouring unjust laws. These were the social evils he opposed.

items.stem: Describe any three causes that led to the Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: Three causes led to the Non-Cooperation Movement. (1) The Rowlatt Act: after the First World War the British government passed this Act, which authorised the arrest and imprisonment of anyone without trial. (2) The Jallianwala Bagh tragedy: on 13 April 1919 General Dyer ordered his troops to open fire without warning on an unarmed crowd that had gathered peacefully at Jallianwala Bagh. (3) The Khilafat issue: after Turkey's defeat in the war the Sultan of Turkey was stripped of his authority, and to restore his position the Khilafat Movement was begun under the Ali Brothers, Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali. Together these grievances pushed Gandhiji and the Congress to launch the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Describe any three causes of ‘Civil Disobedience Movement’.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement grew out of the discontent brewing among Indians. (1) Salt tax: the British monopoly over the production and sale of salt, and the tax on it, was a severe burden on the poor and a stark example of exploitative economic policy. (2) The Simon Commission: sent to India in 1928 to recommend constitutional reforms, it was boycotted and widely criticised because it had no Indian member. (3) The demand for Purna Swaraj: the Congress declaration of complete independence on 26 January 1930 was a direct precursor of the movement. (4) Repression by the British government, including the Rowlatt Act, further fuelled anger and frustration. These factors together sparked the Civil Disobedience Movement.

items.stem: ‘Workers of Assam had their own understanding of Mahatma Gandhi and the nation of Swaraj’. Explain with examples.
items.answer: For the plantation workers of Assam, Swaraj meant the right to move freely in and out of the confined space in which they were enclosed, and it meant keeping a link with the village from which they had come. (1) Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 plantation workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, which was rarely granted. (2) When they heard of the Non-Cooperation Movement, thousands of workers defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home. (3) They believed that Gandhi Raj was coming and that everyone would be given land in their own villages. (4) They never reached their destination; stranded by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by the police and brutally beaten. Thus the workers gave Gandhiji and Swaraj a meaning drawn from their own experience of bondage.

items.stem: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement unfold in the cities and towns of India?
items.answer: In the cities and towns the Non-Cooperation Movement unfolded as follows: (1) it began with the participation of the middle class in the cities; (2) thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges; (3) many teachers resigned their posts; (4) lawyers gave up their legal practices; (5) the council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras; and (6) foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed and foreign cloth burnt in huge bonfires. The movement therefore began in the towns as a boycott of British institutions and goods by the urban middle class.

items.stem: Describe the implications of First World War on the economic and political situation of India.
items.answer: The First World War created a new political and economic situation in India. (1) Defence expenditure increased hugely; customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced to finance the war. (2) Villagers were called upon to supply soldiers, and forced recruitment in rural areas caused widespread resentment. (3) Prices of essential commodities doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing extreme hardship to ordinary people. (4) Crops failed in many parts of India in 1918-19 and 1920-21, resulting in acute food shortages. (5) An influenza epidemic spread, and according to the 1921 census 12-13 million people perished in the famines and epidemics. The war thus deepened economic distress and prepared the ground for a mass national movement.

items.stem: Describe the role of poor peasantry in the ‘Civil Disobedience Movement.’
items.answer: The poor peasantry gave the Civil Disobedience Movement its mass character. (1) Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation, and framed demands wide enough for every class to identify with; the most stirring of them was the abolition of the salt tax. (2) Salt was consumed by rich and poor alike and was one of the most essential items of food, so the tax on it and the government monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule. (3) The poor peasantry was asked to pay more taxes when it could hardly make ends meet; infuriated, peasants came out in huge numbers to support Gandhiji and his followers. It was because of them that the Civil Disobedience Movement could become a mass movement.

items.stem: What do you know about the Lucknow Pact of 1916? Write its importance in history of India.
items.answer: The pact signed between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League at Lucknow in 1916 is known as the Lucknow Pact. The two parties agreed to sink their differences and to give a united fight to the colonial government. Its importance was: (1) it could re-unite the moderate and extremist leaders of the Indian National Congress; (2) controversies between the Congress and the Muslim League were settled amicably; and (3) a united scheme of constitutional reforms was agreed between the Congress and the League, which they decided to place jointly before the British government. The Pact therefore marked a rare moment of Hindu-Muslim political unity in the national movement.

items.stem: Explain with examples the role of industrialists in the freedom struggle of India.
items.answer: After Gandhiji launched the Non-Cooperation Movement: (1) foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt; (2) traders refused to sell foreign goods; and (3) the boycott won wide acceptance at the national level. During this period it was Indian industry that supported the cause, since the demand for Indian goods went up. Industrialists such as Jamnalal Bajaj, J.R.D. Tata and the G.D. Birla group backed the movement and placed the national interest first. Indian industry was still technically primitive, but it supported the national cause to a large extent, while French and London based companies worked to protect their own vested interests and profit margins. The industrialists thus strengthened the freedom struggle by financing it and by making swadeshi goods available.

items.stem: Mention any three shortcomings of the Indian Act of 1919.
items.answer: The Act of 1919 failed to fulfil the aspirations of the people of India; the rules under it were only a means of draining India of her wealth and of prolonging her servitude. Its shortcomings were: (1) power was said to be given to the provinces, but the Governor General in Council at the Centre kept exclusive power to decide affairs of state at his will; (2) it was the Governor-General, and not the courts, who decided whether a particular subject was Central or Provincial; (3) electorates were divided on a communal basis; and (4) dyarchy, a dual system of administration, was introduced in the provinces. The Act therefore conceded no real self-government.

items.stem: Which were the two types of demands mentioned by Gandhi ji in his letter to viceroy Irwin on 31 January 1930. Why was abolitions of salt tax most stirring demand? Explain
items.answer: On 31 January 1930 Mahatma Gandhi wrote a letter to Viceroy Irwin in which he set out the demands of the people: (1) the salt tax should be removed; (2) there should be impartial judgement against the cruel violence of the police on civilians; and (3) the Non-Cooperation Movement should be stopped. The salt demand was the most stirring because the tax affected every civilian, rich and poor alike. Gandhiji wanted to bring members of every section of society into the movement, and since the production of salt was a major part of the government's oppressive activity, the removal of the salt tax was the most powerful of the eleven demands he put before Viceroy Irwin.

items.stem: Explain any three measures taken by the British administration to uprise the movement started against the Rowlatt Act”
items.answer: On 6 April 1919, after the First World War, Indians expected some reward from the British government, but instead the government hurriedly announced the Rowlatt Act without thinking of its repercussions. The Act rested on the denial of ordinary rights: (1) under it revolutionaries could be imprisoned for two years without any reason being given; (2) an imprisoned person could not file a suit in a court against his detention; and (3) no one could assemble at a place against the government's rules or take part in a procession. These repressive measures were how the British administration tried to crush the movement launched against the Rowlatt Act.

items.stem: How could Non-cooperation become a Movement? Give your opinion.
items.answer: Non-cooperation became a movement in the following way. (1) According to Gandhiji it was to unfold in two stages: in the first, titles awarded by the government were to be surrendered and civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods boycotted; in the second, if the government replied with repression, a full civil disobedience campaign would be launched. (2) Through the summer of 1920 Mahatma Gandhi and Shaukat Ali toured extensively to mobilise popular support, and between September and December there was an intense tussle within the Congress between the supporters and the opponents of the movement. (3) The differences were resolved at the Congress session at Nagpur in December 1920, where a compromise was worked out, the Non-cooperation programme was adopted and it took the shape of a mass movement.

items.stem: When and why was the Cripps Mission sent to India? Point out any two main defects responsible for its failure.
items.answer: The Cripps Mission was sent to India in March 1942 under the chairmanship of Sir Stafford Cripps to win the co-operation of the Indian people in the Second World War; the British position in 1942 had become very precarious because of Hitler's attacks, so they wanted Indian support. The talks failed because of two main defects: (1) Cripps rejected the Congress proposal for the formation of a national government during the war; and (2) he was not prepared to give any assurance of granting independence to India even after the war. As a result his proposals were rejected by both the Congress and the Muslim League.

items.stem: What were the three local issues in which Gandhiji experimented his technique of Satyagrah during the years 1917-18 ? How were these issues resolved ? or How did Gandhiji resolve the issue of Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad through his unique method ‘Satyagrah’?
items.answer: Gandhiji tested Satyagraha on three local issues. (1) Champaran Satyagraha: the first experiment, in 1917, was with the indigo farmers of Bihar, who were encouraged to raise their voice against the oppressive rules of the British planters; Gandhiji had their demands sanctioned by an inquiry commission set up for the purpose. (2) Kheda Satyagraha: the second experiment was with the farmers of Kheda in Gujarat, where the British officials were collecting land revenue at the highest rates even after a severe famine and crop failure; finally the revenue was waived and the issue was resolved. (3) Ahmedabad Satyagraha: the third experiment was made with the mill workers of Ahmedabad, where Gandhiji resorted to a fast along with the workers, and the British authorities had to raise wages by up to 35% along with certain reforms in working conditions. In each case peaceful Satyagraha won the demand.

items.stem: Explain any three reasons for the slow-down of Non-cooperation movement in cities.
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement was started by Mahatma Gandhi and, after the Nagpur session of December 1921, all sections joined it; but in the cities it soon slowed down. (1) Everyone had agreed to boycott mill-made cloth, but khadi was not available in sufficient quantity and was thought not to look good, so the rich in the cities did not take to it. (2) Students and teachers wanted to boycott government schools, but the Congress could not open enough alternative schools, so teachers and students trickled back to government institutions. (3) Lawyers who had given up practice faced the problem of what occupation to take up instead, so lawyers and judges went back to their previous work in the government courts. The absence of substitutes for British institutions therefore slowed the movement in the cities.

items.stem: “The two-nation theory was a total falsification of the entire history of the Indian people.” Explain the statement.
items.answer: The two-nation theory falsified Indian history for three reasons. (1) During a long stay and intermixing over thousands of years the Hindus and the Muslims had developed a common culture, especially during medieval times, and had almost become one people. (2) Suffering commonly under one foreign power, they developed many common traits; they fought shoulder to shoulder in the Great uprising of 1857 and were hunted, imprisoned, tried and hanged on a common platform, which made them one people. (3) In the 20th century, when the nationalist movement became a mass movement, all the people were cemented into one nation. The history of India is therefore a history of one people, not of two nations.

items.stem: How did ‘Salt March’ become an effective tool of resistance against colonialism ? Explain.
items.answer: As the demands in his letter to Viceroy Irwin were not fulfilled, Gandhiji began a march from his ashram at Sabarmati to the Gujarat coastal town of Dandi, accompanied by 78 trusted followers. The march continued for 24 days, covering about 10 miles a day, and during it Gandhiji explained the meaning of swaraj to the people and urged them to defy the British laws. On reaching Dandi on 6 April he ceremonially violated the salt law by manufacturing salt from boiling sea water. This was the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement: people were asked to refuse co-operation and to break colonial laws, and thousands broke the salt law and demonstrated in front of government salt factories. In this way the Salt March became an effective tool of resistance against colonialism.

items.stem: Why was the participation of Dalits in the Civil Disobedience Movement limited?
items.answer: Dalit participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement was limited for these reasons. (1) The Congress had for long ignored the Dalits for fear of offending the Sanatanis, the conservative high-caste Hindus. (2) Mahatma Gandhi held that Swaraj would not come for a hundred years if untouchability was not abolished; (3) he called them Harijans, lived with them and himself cleaned toilets to dignify the work of sweepers. (4) Many Dalit leaders, however, demanded reserved seats in educational institutions and a separate electorate rather than Congress-led agitation. For these reasons Dalits did not take part whole-heartedly and their participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement remained limited.

items.stem: The response of the Muslim community was lukewarm to the Civil Disobedience. Why? or “Some of the Muslim political organisations in India were lukeworm in their response to the Civil Disobedience Movement.” Examine the statement.
items.answer: The response of the Muslim community was lukewarm because: (1) after the Non-Cooperation Movement relations between Hindus and Muslims worsened, as each community organised religious processions that provoked communal clashes and riots; (2) Congress members were seen as associates of Hindu religious nationalist groups such as the Hindu Mahasabha; (3) when the Civil Disobedience Movement started there was an atmosphere of suspicion and distrust between the communities, and Muslims feared that they would be submerged under the domination of a Hindu majority in independent India; and (4) there were important differences over the question of representation in the future assemblies that were to be elected. These fears kept most Muslim political organisations away from the movement.

items.stem: In which session of Congress, Non-Cooperation Movement was adopted ? What were the plans of Gandhi to launch Non-Cooperation Movement ?
items.answer: Congress adopted the Non-Cooperation Movement at its Nagpur session in December 1920, on a proposal moved by Gandhi. Gandhi's plan was that the movement should unfold in stages; that titles awarded by the government should be surrendered; that Indians should boycott the civil services, the army, the police, the courts, schools and foreign goods; and that if the government answered with repression, a full Civil Disobedience Movement should be launched. So the movement was adopted at the Nagpur session of December 1920 and was to proceed in these graded stages.

items.stem: Explain any four factors to show how did the First World War help in the growth of the National Movement in India.
items.answer: The First World War fed the national movement in four main ways. First, the heavy loss of men and material created a new political and economic situation in the country. Second, villagers were forcibly recruited into the army and made to do begar during the war, which caused widespread anger among Indians. Third, the war created a huge expenditure on arms, which forced the government to raise revenue by imposing fresh taxes. Fourth, crops failed at the same time and the government gave no support, adding to popular discontent. Together these conditions pushed large numbers of Indians towards the national movement.

items.stem: Explain the idea of Satyagraha.
items.answer: Satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. It suggested that if the cause was true and the struggle was against injustice, then physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor. Without being aggressive, a satyagrahi could win the battle, because the fight was to be won by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor rather than by forcing him to accept truth through violence. Thus Satyagraha was a non-violent method of resisting injustice through the moral force of truth.

items.stem:
What was the Rowlatt Act of 1919 ? Explain the reaction of the people against the Rowlatt Act.
or
How was Rowlatt Act opposed by the people in India? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The Rowlatt Act was an oppressive law passed by the British government in 1919. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed political prisoners to be detained without trial for two years. Indians opposed it strongly: rallies were organised in various cities, workers went on strike on the railways, and workshops and offices were closed down; a peaceful protest meeting was held at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar; Gandhiji started a hartal against the unjust law on 6th April 1919; Dr. Satyapal and Dr. Saif-ud-din Kitchlew were arrested; and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre followed the protest against these arrests.
items.ocr: The printed answer opens with the misprint 'Rowtatt Act'; written here as 'Rowlatt Act' as in the question stem.

items.stem: What was the main issue behind the Khilafat Movement? Why did Gandhiji support this ?
items.answer: At the end of the First World War the Ottoman Turkey was defeated, and there were rumours that a harsh treaty was about to be imposed on the Khalifa, the spiritual head of the Muslims all over the world. The main issue of the Khilafat Movement was therefore to defend the Khalifa's temporal powers, and a Khilafat Committee was formed for this purpose; a few Muslim leaders approached Gandhiji for his support. Gandhiji saw the issue as an opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement, and so he gave his consent to support the movement at the Calcutta session of the Congress.

items.stem: How did the tribals of the ‘Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh’ interpret Swaraj ? What was the differences between the beliefs and practices of their leader, Alluri Sita Ram Raju ?
items.answer: For the tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills, Swaraj meant an end to begar, free access to the forests and non-payment of taxes. Their leader Alluri Sitaram Raju claimed to be inspired by Gandhiji and persuaded people to adopt khadi and give up drinking, yet in practice he asserted the use of violence as a means of struggle. He believed that India could be liberated only by the use of force, and under his leadership the rebels attacked police stations, attempted to kill British officials and carried on guerilla warfare to achieve Swaraj. The difference, therefore, lay between his professed Gandhian belief and his violent practice.

items.stem:
What was the impact of Non-Cooperation Movement on economy ?
or
Describe briefly any three economic effects of Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement had a marked economic effect. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs. 102 crore to Rs. 57 crore. In many places merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or to finance foreign trade. And as more and more people took to wearing Indian cloth, the production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up.

items.stem: Who was Baba Ramchandra ? What were the problems of peasants in Awadh ?
items.answer: Baba Ramchandra was a peasant leader of Awadh, a sanyasi who had earlier gone to Fiji as an indentured labourer; he led the peasant movement against the talukdars and landlords of Awadh. The peasants there suffered on three counts: the talukdars and landlords demanded exorbitantly high rents and a variety of other cesses; the peasants had to do begar, working on the landlords' farms without any payment; and as tenants they had no security of tenure, being regularly evicted so that they could acquire no right over the leased land.

items.stem: Mention three reasons by which the rich peasant communities took active participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement.
items.answer: The rich peasant communities — the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh — joined the Civil Disobedience Movement for these reasons. They grew commercial crops, and when prices fell and trade depression set in, their incomes dropped sharply. As a result they could not meet the government's revenue demands. The government nevertheless refused to reduce the revenue demand. This enraged the rich peasants, who became active in the movement because for them the fight for Swaraj was a struggle against high revenue.
items.ocr: The question asks for three reasons; the printed answer lists four points.

items.stem: Poor peasants kept themselves away from Congress and Civil Disobedience Movement. Why ?
items.answer: The poor peasantry stayed away for the following reasons. They were badly hit by the Economic Depression, most of them working small plots of land rented from landlords. With incomes falling during the Depression they could not pay their rents, and what they wanted was that the unpaid rent be remitted. This created a rift between the poor peasants and the rich landlords, who had already supported the Congress and the Civil Disobedience Movement. Because of this the poor peasants kept away from the Congress and joined instead a variety of radical movements, often led by socialists and communists.

items.stem:
Why did the peasants join the Civil Disobedience Movement in India?
or
Evaluate any three features of the peasant movement during Civil Disobedience Movement in India.
items.answer: Peasants joined the Civil Disobedience Movement because they were hard hit by the economic crisis and the falling prices of cash crops, which made it difficult for them to pay the government revenue and caused widespread anger and resentment. They also joined because of the high rents and the variety of other cesses demanded by the landlords. Their demands were a reduction in revenue, the abolition of begar and the social boycott of oppressive landlords, and they wanted their unpaid rent to the landlords to be remitted.

items.stem:
What prevented the working class from participating in the Civil Disobedience Movement ?
or
State any two hopes and expectations of the industrial working class from the Civil Disobedience Movement. Explain any two reasons why the Congress was not interested in including their demands.
items.answer: Industrialists and businessmen such as Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G.D. Birla had given the Civil Disobedience Movement generous support, and this kept the workers from coming close to the Congress and the movements it launched. Consequently the working class, except in Nagpur, did not take part in the Civil Disobedience Movement, though some workers did adopt Gandhian ideas such as the boycott of foreign goods in their own agitations against low wages and poor working conditions. The Congress, for its part, was reluctant to include workers' demands in its programme of struggle, since these would have run counter to the industrialists' interests and alienated them from active participation.

items.stem:
When did Mahatma Gandhi return from South Africa? State any two important works or Satyagrahas which Mahatma Gandhi did immediately after his arrival in India.
or
How did Mahatma Gandhi successfully organise Satyagraha movements in various places just after arriving in India? Explain by giving three examples.
items.answer: Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in January 1915 and at once took an active part in India's freedom struggle. His method was satyagraha, which emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth, and held that if the cause was true and the fight was against injustice, physical force was not necessary to defeat the oppressor. His early satyagrahas were: in 1916 the Champaran satyagraha in Bihar against the oppressive plantation system; in 1917 a satyagraha in support of the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat; and in 1918 a satyagraha at Ahmedabad among the cotton mill workers.

items.stem:
What was Satyagraha ? Explain the three main Satyagrahas launched by Gandhiji in India.
or
Which three early Satyagrahas were organised by Mahatma Gandhi ?
or
Mention the three movements based on Satyagraha, organised by Mahatma Gandhi on his return to India from South Africa.
items.answer: Satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth; it held that if the cause was true and the fight was against injustice, physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor. The three main satyagrahas launched by Gandhiji in India were: in 1916 he travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system; in 1917 he organised a satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat; and in 1918 he organised a satyagraha among the cotton mill workers of Ahmedabad.

items.stem: Discuss the role of the Muslims in the Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: Because the Congress agreed to run the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements together, the Muslims joined the Congress through their Khilafat Committee. They did not cast their votes in the elections held to the legislature, and they started teaching institutions such as Jamia Millia and the Aligarh Muslim High School. Hakim Ajmal Khan was voted chairman of the Congress, and the great Urdu poet Maulana Hasrat Mohani proposed that Swaraj be defined as complete independence. Later, when the Turkish revolutionaries led by Mustafa Kamal Pasha abolished the Khilafat, the Indian Muslims withdrew their support from the Congress as their purpose had been achieved.

items.stem: ‘Some icons and symbols were used for unifying the people and sparking in them the feeling of nationalism.’ Give two evidences to support above statement.
items.answer: Two pieces of evidence support this. First, the image of Bharat Mata came to be identified with India, the motherland. Abanindranath Tagore painted her as an ascetic figure, calm, composed, divine and spiritual; later artists painted her in different forms, one image showing Bharat Mata with a trishul, standing beside a lion and with an elephant behind her, both symbols of power. Second, the flag became a symbol of nationalism: during the Swadeshi Movement in Bengal a tricolour flag was designed with eight lotus flowers representing the eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon representing Hindus and Muslims, and Gandhiji designed the Swaraj flag in 1921.

items.stem: Compare the images of Bharat Mata in this chapter with the image of Germania in Chapter 1.
items.answer: The image of Germania was the symbol of the German nation, whereas the image of Bharat Mata was the symbol of the Indian nation. Both images inspired nationalists, who worked very hard to unify their respective countries and to attain a liberal nation. They differ, however, in that the image of Bharat Mata reflects the religious basis of its making, while Germania does not. Bharat Mata also became a controversial figure and indirectly played a role in the spread of communalism in pre-independent India, whereas no such controversy was attached to the image of Germania.

items.stem: Write a brief essay on women's participation in the Civil Disobedience, Movement of 1930.
items.answer: In 1930 women took part in the Civil Disobedience Movement on a large scale. During Gandhiji's Salt March thousands of women came out of their homes to listen to him. They joined protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth shops and liquor shops, and many of them went to jail. In the urban areas these women came from high-caste families, while in the rural areas they came from rich peasant households; they regarded service to the nation as a sacred duty of women.

items.stem:
Describe the different factors that shaped the political situation in the late 1920s.
or
Which factors shaped the Indian politics by the late 1920s? Explain.
items.answer: The widespread movement against the Rowlatt Act had been launched, but it was still confined to the cities and towns. Mahatma Gandhi now felt the need to launch a much broader-based movement in India. He was, however, certain that no such movement could be organised without bringing Hindus and Muslims together. One way of doing this, he felt, was to take up the Khilafat issue and use it as an opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement. At the Calcutta Session of the Congress in September 1920 he convinced the leaders of the need to start a Non-Cooperation Movement in support of the Khilafat as well as for Swaraj.

items.stem: How did the Business class relate itself to the Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain with examples.
items.answer: Indian merchants and industrialists were eager to expand their businesses and reacted sharply against colonial policies that restricted their trading activity. They wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a rupee–sterling exchange ratio that would discourage imports. To organise their interests they formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927. Led by prominent industrialists such as Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, they attacked colonial control over the Indian economy and supported the Civil Disobedience Movement, giving financial assistance and refusing to buy or sell imported goods. Most businessmen wanted trade to flourish without constraints, and so they saw swaraj as the condition for their own prosperity and backed the movement.

items.stem: Highlight the reasons for the growth of nationalist tensions in the Balkan region before the First World War.
items.answer: The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism, together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire, made the region explosive; through the nineteenth century the Ottoman Empire tried to strengthen itself through modernisation and internal reforms but with little success. As the different Slavic nationalities struggled to define their identity and win independence, each claiming territory on the basis of past glory, the Balkans became an area of intense conflict. Alongside this, each of the big powers — Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary — was keen on countering the hold of the others over the Balkans and on extending its own control there. This rivalry led to a series of wars in the region and finally to the First World War.

items.stem:
The Civil Disobedience Movement saw the participation of different social classes and groups. Give reasons for the participation of the following:
(1) rich peasants
(2) poor peasants
(3) business classes
(4) industrial working classes
(5) women.
items.answer: Rich peasants: communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh joined because, as producers of commercial crops, they were hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices, and the government's refusal to reduce the revenue demand made them fight against high revenues. Poor peasants: they joined because they found it difficult to pay rent and wanted their unpaid rent to the landlord to be remitted. Business class: they reacted against colonial policies that restricted their activity, wanted protection against imports of foreign goods, and believed swaraj would cancel colonial restrictions so that trade could flourish freely. Industrial working class: they did not participate in large numbers except in the Nagpur region; some workers selectively adopted parts of the Gandhian programme, such as the boycott of foreign goods, as part of their own struggles against low wages and poor working conditions. Women: they took part on a large scale, joining protest marches, manufacturing salt and picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops, and many went to jail. Thus each group joined the movement for reasons rooted in its own grievances against colonial rule.

items.stem: The middle classes played an important role in the Non-Cooperation Movement in the cities. Explain. Why do you think that the movement slowed down in the cities?
items.answer: The middle classes led the movement in the cities. Thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up their legal practices. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. The movement nevertheless slowed down in the cities for several reasons. Khadi cloth was more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it and could not boycott mill cloth for long. Boycotting British institutions also created a problem because there were no alternative national institutions to meet educational and legal needs. As a result students and teachers began trickling back to government schools and lawyers returned to work in government courts, and the urban phase of the movement gradually lost its momentum.

items.stem: How did Non-Cooperation movement start with participation of middle class people in the cities? Explain its impact on the economic front.
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement began in the cities with the middle classes. It was launched by Gandhiji in 1920 to express resentment against actions considered oppressive, such as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Rowlatt Act, and thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges. Teachers and headmasters resigned and lawyers gave up their legal practices. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party, the party of non-Brahmans, felt that entering the council was one way of gaining power. On the economic front the effects were sharp: foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. In many places traders and merchants refused to trade in foreign goods and even refused to finance foreign trade, so that the import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922. As the boycott spread, people used only Indian cloth and discarded foreign clothes, and the production of Indian textile mills and handloom went up greatly.

items.stem: Why did Gandhiji start Non-Cooperation Movement? Explain.
items.answer: Gandhiji started the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1921 for several reasons. He argued that British rule had been established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived only because of that cooperation, so the time had come to withdraw cooperation from the British. After returning from Africa in 1915 he had launched local satyagrahas, but he was looking for an opportunity to begin a national-level movement against the British. The First World War added greatly to the misery of the Indian people, as heavy taxes, high prices, famines and epidemics made life wretched. The British passed the Rowlatt Act despite the opposition of Indian leaders; the Act curbed political activity and allowed the detention of political prisoners. Finally, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the injustice done to Punjab made Indians angry and demanded redress. For these reasons Gandhiji launched the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Why was Congress reluctant to allow women to hold any position of authority within the organisation? How did women participate in Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain.
items.answer: Gandhiji was convinced that it was the duty of a woman to look after her home and family and that women should be good mothers and good wives, and for a long time the Congress was therefore reluctant to allow women to hold any position of authority within the organisation; it was content with a symbolic presence of women. Women nevertheless participated in the Civil Disobedience Movement in large numbers. During Gandhiji's Salt March thousands of women came out of their houses to listen to him. They joined protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops. Many were arrested and sent to jail. In urban areas these women came from high-caste families — for example Sarojini Naidu, Satyavati Devi and Kamla Nehru — while in rural areas they came from rich peasant households. Women broke open the doors of shops, came out on the roads and helped the movement's leaders. In Bombay a large section of Gujarati women, influenced by Gandhiji's idealism, took part in the national movement, and Bengal, the nerve centre of female education in India, saw increased participation, with women rallying before Bethune College, Calcutta in 1930 in support of the movement.

items.stem: Why did Gandhi decide to launch a nationwide ‘Satyagraha’ against the proposed Rowlatt Act (1919)? How was it opposed? Explain.
items.answer: The Rowlatt Act was passed in spite of the united opposition of the Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. It gave the government enormous powers to suppress political agitation and allowed the detention of political prisoners without trial for two years, with no provision for appeal. The passing of such an unjust law aroused large-scale indignation, and Gandhiji, who had already formed a Satyagraha Sabha, therefore decided to call for a country-wide protest against it. Throughout the country 6 April 1919 was observed as a National Humiliation Day. Gandhiji wanted non-violent civil disobedience against such unjust laws, so hartals and rallies were organised in various cities, workers went on strike in railway workshops and shops were closed down. Communication, railway and telegraph lines were disrupted. The movement remained non-violent yet proved highly effective in opposing the Act.

items.stem: Why was the ‘Salt March’ considered an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism? Explain.
items.answer: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the whole nation. On 31 January 1930 he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, one of which was the abolition of the salt tax. Salt was one of the most essential food items, consumed by rich and poor alike, and the tax on it together with the government monopoly over its production was regarded as an oppression on the people. Gandhiji's letter was an ultimatum: if his demands were not met by 11 March he would launch a civil disobedience campaign. When no reply came, he began his famous Salt March with 78 trusted volunteers, walking over 240 miles from his ashram at Sabarmati to the Gujarati coastal town of Dandi. The volunteers marched for 24 days, about 10 miles a day, and thousands came to hear Gandhiji wherever he stopped, where he explained what he meant by swaraj and urged people to peacefully defy the British. On 6 April he reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law by manufacturing salt from sea water, and this act, which touched every Indian household, marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement and made the Salt March an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism.

items.stem: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement spread to the countryside and drew into its fold the struggles of peasants and tribal communities? Elaborate.
items.answer: From the cities the Non-Cooperation Movement spread into the countryside and drew the struggles of peasants and tribals into its fold. In Awadh the peasants' movement was led by Baba Ramchandra against talukdars and landlords who demanded extremely high rents and a variety of other cesses, and who forced peasants to work on their farms without any payment (begar). Peasants had no security of tenure and were regularly evicted so that they could acquire no right over the leased land; their demands were a reduction of revenue, the abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords. In 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru began talking to the villagers and the Oudh Kisan Sabha was formed, and within a month 300 branches had been set up in the villages. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s against the closure of forest areas by the colonial government, which prevented tribal people from entering the forests to graze cattle or collect fuelwood and fruits; they felt that their traditional rights were being denied. When the government forced them to contribute begar for road building, the hill people revolted. Their leader Alluri Sitaram Raju, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking, though he asserted that India could be liberated only by the use of force. In this way the movement acquired a rural and tribal dimension.

items.stem: How had the ‘First World War’ created economic problems in India? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The First World War created serious economic problems in India. It led to a huge increase in defence expenditure, which was financed by raising taxes and increasing custom duties. During the war years crop failure resulted in an acute shortage of food. Food prices rose sharply, almost doubling between 1913 and 1918, which increased the hardships of the people. Villages were called upon to supply soldiers, and in some rural areas the colonial government forced people to join the army, causing widespread resentment and anger and setting the stage for depression. On top of this an influenza epidemic spread and added to the hardships of the people, while the war weakened the gold standard. Thus the war brought high prices, scarcity, forced recruitment and disease, creating deep economic distress in India.
items.concept: Impact of the First World War

items.stem: “The Civil Disobedience Movement was different from the Non-co-operation Movement.” Support the statement with examples.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement was a movement of open defiance of British law, launched by Mahatma Gandhi in April 1930, and it differed from the Non-Cooperation Movement in several ways. It was a unique movement because Gandhiji found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation against the government monopoly over its production; the issue of salt looked ordinary at first but proved the most stirring one. In the Non-Cooperation Movement people were asked only to refuse cooperation with the British, whereas in the Civil Disobedience Movement they were asked not merely to deny cooperation but also to break colonial laws. The movement spread like wildfire and re-energised all classes of the nation: the salt law was broken, foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops were picketed, and peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes. Another important feature was the large-scale participation of women; thousands of women came out of their homes, joined protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops. These features show that the Civil Disobedience Movement went well beyond the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi find in ‘salt’ a powerful symbol that could unite the nation? Explain.
items.answer: Salt was a commodity consumed by every individual, rich and poor alike, and its stock in the seas and oceans was undepleting, so it was a gross atrocity on the part of the British Government to impose a tax on it and take its production under a state monopoly. Salt therefore offered an excellent opportunity to expose the malafide intention of the foreign government before the masses of India. Acting on this, Gandhiji sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands. The demands were wide ranging, some general and some specific, and concerned the interests of all sections of Indian society; the removal of the tax on salt was one of them. He specifically stated that if the Government appeared unwilling to negotiate on the demands by 11 March, the Congress would launch a civil disobedience campaign. As the British government gave no response, Gandhi launched the Dandi March, a 375 km march from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal town of Dandi in Gujarat. On these counts salt became an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism, gathering nationwide support of the Indian masses and openly challenging British laws.
items.ocr: The book prints the Dandi March as beginning on 13th March 1930 and as a 375 km march; both figures are reproduced from the printed solution although other questions in the same chapter print 12 March and 240 miles.

items.stem: How did the Civil Disobedience Movement come into force in various parts of the country? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement drew in different groups across the country, each for its own reasons. In the countryside the rich peasants of Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh were active in the movement; badly hit by the trade depression and falling prices, they became enthusiastic supporters. Many of the poor peasants were small tenants cultivating land rented from landlords, and as the depression continued they found it difficult to pay their rent, so they joined a variety of radical movements, often led by socialists and communists. The business classes reacted against colonial policies during the movement; wanting protection against imports of foreign goods, they supported the movement and refused to buy or sell imported goods. The movement also witnessed the large-scale participation of women, who came out of their homes, joined protest marches and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops, and many of them went to jail. The plantation workers in Assam defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home, believing that Gandhi Raj was near and that everyone would be given land in their own villages. In this way the movement came into force in different regions and among different social groups across India.

items.stem: Why was the Non-Cooperation Movement launched in 1920? Why did Gandhiji call off the movement in 1922?
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) was launched for several causes. There was a breach of trust committed by the British Government after the First World War, the enforcement of the Rowlatt Act, the unruly killing of peaceful demonstrators at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar in Punjab, and the so-called biased reforms effected through the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms. Dyarchy was introduced in the Bengal province under those same reforms. The dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire in Turkey, with the Khalifa disowned, angered Indian Muslims and brought the Khilafat cause into the movement. The movement came to a sudden halt in 1922. Things went out of hand when the police at Chauri-Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh fired at Congress volunteers and the infuriated mob, in retaliation, set the police station on fire and killed 22 policemen. Because the movement had turned violent, Gandhiji immediately suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Describe the Peasant Rebellion in Awadh during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: The peasants of Awadh during the movement were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier worked in Fiji as an indentured labourer. The peasants' movement was started to demand a reduction of revenue, the abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords. During the movement Nai-Dhobi bandhs were organised at many places, so as to deprive the landlords even of the services of washermen and barbers. The movement was directed against the taluqdars and landlords who charged high revenue from the peasants. In 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru formed the Oudh Kisan Sabha to help the peasants free themselves from the clutches of the landlords, and within a month 300 branches had been set up in the villages. The movement spread quickly, and in 1921 the houses of taluqdars and merchants were attacked, bazaars were looted and grain hoards were taken over. Thus the Awadh peasant rebellion became a militant rural wing of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem:
How did Gandhiji bring the masses into the National Movement?
or
How as the freedom struggle for India’s independence was converted into a Mass movement by M. K. Gandhi?
items.answer: Gandhiji's simple, saintly life and his habit of convincing the masses in their local languages made him extremely popular as a leader. His undisputed leadership and magnetic personality helped to coordinate and unite the movement. His policy of non-violent satyagraha brought millions into the struggle; the Champaran satyagraha, for instance, brought the peasants in. He launched three powerful mass movements — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India — which influenced millions of Indians of every section of society to show bravery, self-confidence and revolutionary passive resistance against British rule. His new methods of agitation, such as hartals, boycott, civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes, appealed to ordinary people. Under his guidance Indians withstood brutal repression and willingly accepted imprisonment, lathi charges and bullets for the sake of freedom. Through his programmes of social reform, the charkha, cottage industries and his fight against untouchability, the Harijans and depressed classes joined the freedom struggle and millions gained employment. His deep commitment to Hindu-Muslim unity and his secular ideals persuaded every community to unite for the noble cause of freedom. His support to the Ahmedabad mill workers' strike in 1918 and his satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act kept him in close touch with the masses, and he became the Father of the Nation. He was the first Indian nationalist leader who identified his life and manner of living with that of the common people and earned the title of ‘Mahatma’. In these ways Gandhiji converted the freedom struggle into a genuine mass movement.

items.stem: Assess the role of Mahatma Gandhi in the National Movement with special reference to the methods adopted by him.
items.answer: When India was ruled by the British the Indians were oppressed directly and indirectly. Mahatma Gandhi arrived from South Africa, studied Indian conditions thoroughly and used non-violence to improve the condition of Indians, placing his views before the people and his demands before the British. The important movements he led were: (1) The Salt March - on 12 March 1930 Gandhiji marched from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad, to Dandi on the coastal belt of Gujarat, about 240 km away. Thousands came to meet him, and the march marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement against the British Government. (2) Champaran - he launched a satyagraha to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system. (3) Kheda - he launched the Kheda Satyagraha to support peasants who could not pay the revenue because of crop failure. (4) Role of women in the Civil Disobedience Movement - Gandhi made a special appeal to women to stop people from going to shops selling foreign cloth and liquor; women joined the protest marches, and even rural women from rich families came out to join. (5) In 1918 he intervened in the Ahmedabad mill workers' strike and helped them get their pay raised, for which he undertook a fast unto death. Through these methods - satyagraha, non-violence, fasting, boycott and mass marches - Gandhiji gave the national movement both a moral force and a mass base.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi decide to launch a nationwide Satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act? Explain any three reasons.
items.answer: Indians were outraged by the Rowlatt Act of 1919, and Gandhiji decided to launch a nationwide satyagraha against it for these reasons. (1) People had hoped that after the war their hardships would be over and that the government would take steps to improve their condition. (2) Instead, the government got the Rowlatt Act passed in the Imperial Legislative Council against the united opposition of the Indian members. (3) The Act gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed the detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. (4) These provisions meant the suspension of two principles of justice - trial by jury and habeas corpus - which safeguard people against illegal imprisonment. (5) The Act was therefore regarded as a black law, and Indians under Gandhiji's leadership decided to oppose it. Hence a nationwide satyagraha, beginning with a hartal on 6 April 1919, was launched against the Rowlatt Act.

items.stem: Describe the incident and impact of the Jallianwala Bagh.
items.answer: The events leading to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre were as follows. (1) In March 1919 the Rowlatt Act was passed despite the united opposition of the Indian members; it gave the government power to detain political prisoners without trial for two years. (2) Gandhiji decided to start non-violent civil disobedience against the Act with a hartal on 6 April 1919. (3) On 10 April 1919 the police fired on a peaceful procession in Amritsar, which led to widespread attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations. (4) On 12 April 1919 martial law was imposed and General Dyer took command; he entered the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh, blocked the exits and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds. Effects: (1) After the massacre crowds took to the streets in many north Indian towns, where there were strikes, clashes with the police and attacks on government buildings. (2) The government answered with a policy of repression - satyagrahis were forced to rub their noses on the ground, made to crawl on the streets and salaam all sahibs, people were flogged and villages around Gujranwala in Punjab were bombed. As the violence spread, Gandhiji called off the movement.

items.stem:
"Method of reinterpretation of history was followed to encourage the feeling of nationalism." Give any three arguments to support this statement.
or
How did the 'Reinterpretation of history' created a feeling of nationalism in India ? Give four points.
items.answer: Reinterpretations of history created a feeling of nationalism in India in the following ways. (1) By the end of the nineteenth century many Indians began to feel that, in order to instil a sense of pride in the nation, Indian history had to be thought about differently. (2) The British saw Indians as backward and primitive and incapable of governing themselves; in response Indians began looking into the past to discover India's great achievements. (3) They wrote about the glorious developments of ancient times, when art and architecture, science and mathematics, religion and culture, law and philosophy, crafts and trade had all flourished. (4) This glorious age, in their view, was followed by a history of decline, which began when India was colonised. (5) These nationalist histories urged readers to take pride in India's great achievements of the past and to struggle to change the miserable conditions of life under British rule. Thus rewriting the past became a way of building national pride and a feeling of nationalism.

items.stem: How did the people belonging to different communities, regions or languages develop a sense of collective belonging during the Indian freedom struggle ?
items.answer: Through a variety of cultural processes, people belonging to different communities, regions and languages came to develop a sense of collective belonging. (1) Images: Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata, portrayed as an ascetic figure who is calm, composed, divine and spiritual; devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one's nationalism. (2) Songs: in the 1870s Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland, later included in his novel Anandamath, and it was widely sung during the Swadeshi Movement in Bengal. (3) Folklore: historians recorded folktales and folksongs which gave a true picture of a traditional culture that had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces, and preserving them was essential to restore a sense of pride. (4) Flags: during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal a tricolour flag (red, green and yellow) was designed, and by 1921 Gandhiji had designed the swaraj flag; carrying the flag aloft during marches became a symbol of defiance. (5) Reinterpretation of history: Indian historians wrote about the glorious development of ancient times, when art and architecture, science and mathematics, religion and culture, law and philosophy, craft and trade had flourished, and argued that all this had declined because of the policies of the colonial government. These cultural processes together gave Indians of every region and community a shared sense of being one nation.

items.stem:
"Ideas of nationalism also developed through a movement to revive Indian folklore." Support the statement with four examples.
or
How did the idea of nationalism develop through a movement to revive Indian folklore ? Give three points.
items.answer: Nationalism developed through the revival of Indian folklore in the following ways. (1) Nationalists gathered Indian folktales sung by bards, as well as legends. (2) They felt the need to preserve this folk tradition in order to discover the national character and restore a sense of pride in one's own past. (3) In Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore began collecting ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, and led the movement for folk revival. (4) In Madras, Natesa Sastri published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales, 'The Folklore of Southern India'; he believed folklore was national literature and the most trustworthy record of people's thoughts and characteristics. (5) Nationalists travelled to the villages to gather folk songs, folk tales and legends, which they considered to give a true picture of a tradition and culture that had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces. In this way the revival of folklore helped forge a national identity rooted in the people's own past.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi perceive 'salt' as a powerful symbol that can unite the nation ?
items.answer: Mahatma Gandhi perceived salt as a powerful and effective symbol of resistance against colonialism, and one that could unite the nation, for the following reasons. (1) Salt was consumed by the rich and the poor alike, so it touched every Indian. (2) It was one of the most essential ingredients of food in India. (3) According to Gandhiji, the tax on salt and the government's monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule. (4) By the successful Salt March he showed down the British colonial government in his own satyagraha way. (5) The Salt March was indeed the most significant symbol of resistance against colonialism; the breaking of the salt law had a far-reaching effect, and thereafter all other British symbols became targets of popular anger. Salt therefore became the one issue on which the whole nation could be brought together.

items.stem:
Explain the Khilafat Movement. Why did Gandhiji consider it important to support the Khilafat Movement ?
or
Why did Gandhiji decide to launch a nationwide Satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act, 1919? Explain.
or
Explain the issue behind the Khilafat Movement.
items.answer: The Khilafat issue arose out of the settlement that followed the First World War. (1) The First World War had ended with the defeat of Ottoman Turkey. (2) There were rumours that a harsh peace treaty was going to be imposed on the Ottoman emperor, the spiritual head of the Islamic world (the Khalifa). (3) To defend the Khalifa's temporal powers, a Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919. (4) After the Rowlatt Act, Mahatma Gandhi felt the need to launch a widespread movement in India. (5) He felt that to bring Hindus and Muslims closer together he must take up the Khilafat issue. (6) The Muslim leaders Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali began discussing with Gandhiji the possibility of a united mass action on the issue. (7) Later, at the Calcutta session of September 1920, Gandhiji convinced the Congress leaders to start a Non-Cooperation Movement in support of the Khilafat as well as for swaraj. Gandhiji therefore supported the Khilafat Movement because it offered the chance to unite Hindus and Muslims in a single national struggle.

items.stem:
Trace the events that led to Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar. What was its impact on the Dalits ?
or
Examine the background of the Poona Pact of 1932 in the light of differences between Gandhiji and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
or
Explain the background of the Poona Pact of 1932.
items.answer: The Poona Pact grew out of the differences between Gandhiji and Dr B. R. Ambedkar over the political treatment of the Dalits. (1) The Congress had largely ignored the inclusion of the untouchables or Dalits till 1930. (2) The Congress feared offending the conservative high-caste Hindus within its own fold. (3) Many Dalit leaders were keen on a different political solution to the problems of their community. (4) They believed that political empowerment would resolve the problem of their social disability. (5) Ambedkar organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded a separate electorate for them at the Second Round Table Conference. (6) The issue between Gandhi and Ambedkar over separate electorates for the Dalits was finally resolved under the Poona Pact of September 1932, which gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in the provincial and central legislative councils but kept them within the general (Hindu) electorate. (7) Mahatma Gandhi gave the Dalits the name Harijan and worked for a better place for them in society. The Pact thus won the Dalits guaranteed political representation while keeping the Hindu electorate undivided.
